timeline.description: Martin Breslauer builds an internationally renowned antiquarian bookstore and becomes the heart and soul of Berlin's Bibliophile Society.
timeline.longDescription: On February 4, 1898, Martin Breslauer and his former school friend Edmund Meyer founded the antiquarian and retail bookstore Breslauer & Meyer at Potsdamer Strasse 27b. After the partners parted company in 1904, Breslauer took premises at Unter den Linden 16 and, on his return from the western front in 1918, moved the bookstore to Französische Strasse 46. He was co-founder and board member of the Bibliophile Society and founding member of the Maximilian Society; his bookstore became a hub for Berlin's bibliophiles. Appointed consultant to the Prussian State Library, in 1919 he appraised the private library of Frederick the Great at Sanssouci. In 1929 he discovered the library of Napoleon's second wife Marie Louise in Vienna, and in 1931 handled his largest transaction – the sale of the Prince of Stolberg-Wernigerode's library of 120,000 volumes.

timeline.description: The family is forced from its home, his son is threatened at school, and the Reich Culture Chamber demands the business be handed to 'a suitable Aryan person'.
timeline.longDescription: After 1933 Martin Breslauer very soon encountered difficulties in his private and professional life. In 1934 the family had to give up their elegant suburban house in Lichterfelde and move to an inner-city apartment at Meineke Strasse 16-17. In 1935 his son Bernd was exposed to such serious anti-Semitic threats in the school yard that he did not go back. Faced with expulsion from the Reich Culture Chamber – which would have cost him his license to trade books – Breslauer filed an objection on December 14, 1935. On June 29, 1936, he was told his expulsion could be postponed 'out of consideration for the significance of [his] work' on condition that he hand over his business 'without delay [...] to a suitable Aryan person'. His friend and business associate Martin Bodmer in Switzerland bought most of his famous 21,000-volume library – the largest private bibliographic collection in the world. A punitive tax audit reaching back to 1924 calculated a liability of exactly the amount he would have been able to transfer abroad; he was left with nothing from the sale.

timeline.description: Breslauer closes the business and flees with his family by night train via Holland to England, making a modest new start in London.
timeline.longDescription: Breslauer closed the business as demanded in early 1937 and traveled with his family by night train via Holland to England. To pay for the train tickets, they pawned some golden desert spoons – his son took them to the Berlin pawnshop Schaper to save his father the embarrassment. He was able to take the remaining 6,000 books to London thanks to colleagues who assessed them as worthless for the tax authorities. In December 1938 he obtained official permission to set up an antiquarian bookstore in London. Business, however, was slow.

timeline.description: A German aerial bomb explodes behind the family's London home; Martin Breslauer dies of the shock. His son Bernard later revives the business.
timeline.longDescription: On October 16, 1940, a German aerial bomb exploded in the backyard of Bedford Court Mansions in Bloomsbury where the family lived. Martin Breslauer died a few hours later, aged 69, of a heart attack caused by the shock. His son Bernd – now Bernard – volunteered for military service and spent the war working for British intelligence.

timeline.description: Bernard Breslauer rebuilds the Antiquariat to international renown in London and New York. Today The Regent Berlin hotel stands at Französische Strasse 46.
timeline.longDescription:
When the war ended, Bernard Breslauer managed to build on his father's reputation to establish an antiquarian bookstore of international renown, retaining the name Antiquariat Martin Breslauer. Attempts to reopen the business in Berlin failed, and he stayed in London until moving the business to New York in 1977. He specialized in manuscripts, early prints, illumination and historical bibliography; in 1978 he bought a copy of the Gutenberg bible at auction for the library of the Land Württemberg for 2.2 million dollars – the highest price ever paid for a book at the time. In 1997 he was made an honorary doctor of the Free University Berlin. Bernard Breslauer died aged 86 in 2004, leaving his personal estate to the Berlin State Library; in 2005, Christie's auctioned his valuable library of about 2000 volumes.

The site today

Today The Regent Berlin hotel is located at Französische Strasse 46, where Martin Breslauer's bookstore once stood.
